name: view-helper
intent: Keep a view free of processing logic by giving it dedicated helpers - objects or functions that adapt and format the model it displays - so markup and presentation logic can change independently.
problem: A template needs more than plain property access (currency and date formatting, plurals, derived labels, repeated fragments) and there is no place to put that logic: written inline as scriptlets, template-language expressions or duplicated markup conditionals, it makes the view unreadable and untestable, cannot be reused by another page, and forces whoever edits markup to edit program logic.
context: Server-side presentation code whose views are authored in a template language (JSP, Razor, Thymeleaf, Django/Jinja, ERB, Handlebars, Twirl, Leaf) over dynamic business data. It applies with or without a Front Controller, and pays off most where markup is owned by a different role than the business objects and where several views need the same formatting or adaptation.
benefits: Formatting and model adaptation live in one reusable place: several views - and often several channels (HTML page, mail, PDF, export) - call the same helper instead of re-implementing the logic in markup.
Templates stay declarative: a designer can read and change markup without meeting business code, and web production and application development stop editing the same artifact.
Helpers are ordinary units of code (functions, tag classes, modules), so they are testable without rendering a page.
Model adaptation becomes explicit: the helper decides what the view sees - formatted strings, derived labels, ready-made rows - so the view never walks the raw domain graph.
Logic factored out of a view is reused by calling it, whereas logic embedded in a view can only be reused by copy-and-paste.
tradeoffs: The helper set becomes an API: every template depends on helper names and argument shapes, so changing one either breaks the build (compiled templates) or fails at render time (name-resolved helpers).
Helpers attract responsibilities: because they can reach services, they tend to grow into objects that fetch, cache and format data, recreating the coupling the pattern was meant to remove.

Failures move to render time wherever helper lookup is dynamic: a missing registration, a typo or a wrong argument type surfaces while a page is being rendered, often in production rather than in tests.
Markup-producing helpers must opt out of the engine's escaping (SafeString, Html(...), html_safe, @Html.Raw, UnsafeUnescapedLeafTag), and that opt-out is the standard route for cross-site scripting.
A helper invoked once per row invites hidden I/O: a presentation helper that also retrieves data turns one page render into N queries or remote calls.
Helper registries are frequently process-global (a shared Handlebars instance, app.locals, an environment's filter map), so tests must scope or reset them or helpers leak between cases.

participants.responsibility: The template or page that displays the model; it contains markup plus helper invocations, never the processing logic itself.
Encapsulates one piece of view processing - formatting a value, adapting a model into display shape, driving a repeated fragment - and is invoked from the view or a controller.
A helper that additionally holds the intermediate model state the view renders (the source's name for a helper that carries data rather than only formatting it).
The service the helper - usually through a delegate - asks for the data the view will display.
The recommended access path from helpers to business services, hiding lookup, transport and exceptions; often itself written as another helper.

use_cases: Product, invoice and account pages that must present money, dates, quantities and plurals consistently across many views.
The same data rendered for several channels - HTML, transactional mail, PDF, export - where formatting helpers are shared and only markup differs.
Legacy JSP/servlet views dominated by scriptlets, migrated to helper beans or custom tags one element at a time.
Design-team-owned templates where markup changes often and a markup change must not require touching application code.
Table and row rendering where a helper turns a domain object into cells, keeping loops and conditions out of the view language.
Dashboards that aggregate several services behind a delegate and hand the view a presentation-shaped value bean.

Rails Action View: helper modules mixed into the view context - built-in number, date, link, asset and capture helpers plus the application's own modules under app/helpers - are the View Helper realized as a framework default.

Django: custom template filters and tags implemented in Python, registered with a Library in an app's templatetags module and loaded with {% load %} - the sanctioned place for currency, date and derived-label formatting that the template language deliberately refuses to do.

ASP.NET Core Razor: tag helpers (ITagHelper classes targeting elements or attributes, scoped per view with @addTagHelper) and HTML helper extension methods generate markup so pages stay HTML-friendly instead of C#-heavy.
avoid_when: The template only interpolates values that need no formatting or adaptation; plain property access is clearer than a helper call.
The logic is common to many requests rather than to a view (authentication, logging, locale negotiation) - put it in an Intercepting Filter or Front Controller instead.
The rule is a business rule about the domain (tax, discount, eligibility): it belongs in the model or a presentation model, not in a view helper.
The stack renders through code rather than templates (JSX components, a typed builder DSL) and already enforces the separation; adding a helper layer only deepens the call graph.
A one-off page or throwaway internal tool where two inline expressions are cheaper to own than a helper API.
anti_patterns: Scriptlets or business code inside the view - data access, loops over domain graphs and conditionals written in the template language - which is the problem the pattern exists to remove.
The fat helper: one object that fetches, caches, formats and holds per-request state, so the view now depends on a god object instead of the model.
Helpers that assemble HTML by string concatenation without the engine's escaping API, making every call site an XSS review.
Copy-pasted helper code per view, re-implementing the same formatting locally - the reuse problem the pattern prevents.
Helpers used as a back channel: writing to request/session state or emitting side effects during rendering, so rendering order starts to matter.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: processing and formatting logic is separated from markup.
Single responsibility: one helper presents one thing and does not also retrieve it.
Information hiding: the helper exposes the shape the view needs and hides the domain graph.
DRY: logic factored into a helper is reused by calling it, not by copying markup.
Open/closed: new views reuse existing helpers; adding a view does not change them.
Least knowledge: the view knows helper names, not services, connections or transactions.
best_practices: Keep helpers free of request, session and connection state: pass everything in as arguments so they stay pure and testable.
Let the engine escape: return plain values or use the engine's safe-marking API explicitly, and never concatenate markup from user input by hand.
Name helpers after the presentation intent (money, time_ago, initials) rather than after the data source.
Put retrieval behind a business delegate or facade and keep helpers to adaptation and formatting.
Register helpers in exactly one place (registry, module load, tag library descriptor, template-imports file) so every view resolves the same set.
Bound helper work per row: no queries, remote calls or file access inside a helper that renders within a loop.
sources: Alur, Crupi & Malks, Core J2EE Patterns: Best Practices and Design Strategies, 2nd ed. (2003) - View Helper (Presentation Tier).
